extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP policymakers and practitioners assessing prior art disclosure
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for what counts as prior art disclosure in patent law (effects on novelty and inventive step), including means, timing, place, persons involved, evidentiary requirements and special issues for electronic media/the Internet, as discussed by national AIPPI groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art disclosure on novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure can be adverse to patentability. For novelty, generally all elements of the claimed invention must be disclosed in a single document; for inventive step (obviousness), several pieces of prior art may be combined to demonstrate non‑obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty: require that a single prior document disclose all claim elements. Inventive step: multiple prior art items may be relied upon and combined. National examples: Brazil, Bulgaria and Canada all distinguish novelty (single-document) from inventive step (combination permitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pending/unpublished applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending applications that have not yet been published may affect novelty but generally do not affect inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional specifics: Brazil treats contents of an application filed in Brazil (once published) as state of the art from filing or priority date. Canada: pending applications filed in Canada by others may be prior art for novelty under s.28.2(c)/(d) but do not affect inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'state of the art' / prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art comprises everything made accessible to the public prior to the filing date by written or oral description, by use or any other way, in the country or abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil: Article 11 explicitly defines state of the art as anything accessible to the public by any means. Bulgaria provides a similar all‑means definition in law/regulation. Canada has no single statutory definition but treats prior art as material 'available to the public'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized means of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognized means include written publications, oral publications, public use, disclosure by exhibition, and other manners (including electronic means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative practice often favors documentary evidence. Oral testimony alone is generally insufficient unless supported by documentary proof of date and content. Undated pamphlets and blueprints are unacceptable without proof of date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of disclosure (relevance and grace periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is relevant if it occurred prior to the filing date or earliest priority date (subject to statutory grace periods); otherwise it should not affect novelty or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil: disclosure before filing/priority destroys novelty unless within a 12‑month grace period for certain inventor-related disclosures. Canada: statutory timing limits and one‑year grace provisions apply (detailed in s.28.2/28.3). Courts may give less weight to very old prior art never put into practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure (territorial relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the place where information was disclosed is irrelevant: prior art worldwide can be relevant for novelty and inventive step; the applicable law for determining whether disclosure occurred is the law of the country assessing novelty/inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil and Canada treat disclosures abroad as part of the state of the art. Determination of place may be relevant only when proof of accessibility depends on location; accidental vs intentional disclosure makes no difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of discloser and confidentiality implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Who disclosed the information (inventor, applicant, third party) affects whether the disclosure is excluded from the state of the art (e.g., grace periods) and legal remedies for breach of confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil: 12‑month grace period for disclosures by inventor, PTO (in certain circumstances) or third parties who obtained the information from the inventor. A disclosure under confidentiality may not be considered public; breach of confidentiality gives contractual remedies but disclosure older than the grace period destroys novelty. Errors in disclosures are assessed by materiality: if error prevents identification, it may not count as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient, public accessibility and ability to understand
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure requires that information be made accessible to the public; there are generally no statutory requirements on the public's ability to understand the information, but inventive step is judged by what a person skilled in the art would infer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional steps requiring particular expertise (e.g., complex reverse engineering) are necessary to access the information, it may not be considered accessible to the public. If the additional steps are routine/non‑specialized, components visible via ordinary inspection may be accessible prior art. Confidential or implied confidentiality to the recipient can exclude accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic / Internet disclosures generally sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperless information (e.g., on electronic networks or the Internet) can constitute sufficient disclosure to affect novelty or inventive step if it was accessible to the public at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law often does not specifically address Internet disclosures; the main difficulty is documentary proof of date and content. Examples of evidence: accessing a website in presence of a notary, printing a hard copy, and obtaining a notary declaration. E‑mail to an unlimited number of persons constitutes prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and access controls for online material
rubrics_metrics.description: Encryption, password protection or payment requirements affect whether online material is 'accessible to the public'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encrypted information is not accessible to the public. Password‑protected content is not accessible if password access is restricted. Paid access is treated as accessible provided the cost is not so high as to be a true obstacle to access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and duration requirements for online disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: If online information was available during a period sufficient to enable the public to produce evidence of its content and date, the disclosure is part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archiving and preservation (e.g., cached copies, archives) are desirable to support evidentiary proof. Transitory visibility that cannot be evidenced may raise problems of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for Internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Interested third parties challenging novelty/inventive step bear the burden of proving a specific piece of information was disclosed on the Internet; the level of evidence should be the same as for other sources of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no special legal rules for Internet prior art; parties must provide clear evidence of content and date, and documentary veracity must be attested. Administrative and judicial practice require demonstrable documentary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability / 'diligent search' test (Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art must be discoverable by a person skilled in the art conducting a diligent search to be treated as available to the public for relevance purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian cases apply an objective test: whether the hypothetical skilled worker could reasonably be assumed to have knowledge of such prior art; discoverability affects what prior art is treated as part of the skilled person's common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty test (single‑publication/enablement requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For novelty, a single prior publication must disclose the subject‑matter of the claim so clearly that a skilled person could produce the claimed invention without exercise of inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian articulation (Beloit / Free World Trust): the prior publication must contain so clear a direction that a skilled person reading and following it would in every case and without possibility of error be led to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / obviousness test
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is assessed by asking whether an unimaginative skilled technician, in light of general knowledge and information available at the date, would have been led directly and without difficulty to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art relevant to obviousness can be combined; the test focuses on whether the skilled person would be led to the invention rather than whether all elements are present in a single document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure by use / public use criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use or sale can constitute disclosure if made available without restriction to at least one member of the public and the invention's subject matter is capable of being derived (e.g., by observation or reverse engineering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to show that the product was actually dissected or reverse engineered; capability to derive the invention suffices. Courts examine whether the use made the invention accessible to members of the public.
